records.summary: Recommend a regularization strategy based on design matrix diagnostics.
records.dejargonized_summary: Choose between no penalty, Ridge, Lasso, or ElasticNet based on how ill-conditioned and correlated the features are.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The penalty type that best stabilizes the model given the feature geometry.

provenance_notes: kappa(X) > 30 threshold: above this the ratio of largest to smallest singular values forces OLS standard errors to inflate and parameter estimates to become hypersensitive to noise (Hoerl & Kennard 1970).
n > 2k*log(p-k) threshold: below this sample size the probability of successful L1 sparsity recovery converges to zero for Gaussian ensembles (Wainwright 2009).
mu <= 1 mutual incoherence limit: the sharp boundary where Lasso can provably recover the true sparse support in Gaussian ensembles.
Ridge adds lambda*I to the diagonal, shifting condition number from kappa to kappa/(1+lambda), guaranteeing finiteness even for singular X'X.
ElasticNet overcomes Lasso's n-feature saturation limit when p > n by combining L1+L2 to induce the grouping effect for correlated features.
uncertainty_notes: Lasso fails catastrophically when the irrepresentable condition is strongly violated: if inactive features can be heavily represented by linear combinations of active features, Lasso selection consistency drops to near zero and it operates as a screening operator only.

In ultra-high dimensional settings (p >> n, e.g. genomics), computing full SVD for condition number is prohibitive; must bypass exact decomposition and rely on iterative ElasticNet or fast coordinate descent.
When p > n, Lasso is algebraically constrained to select at most n features before saturating, regardless of true sparsity.
Mutual incoherence boundary is sharp for Gaussian ensembles but only approximate for real-world feature distributions.

records.summary: Recommend a loss function based on tail heaviness of target and residuals.
records.dejargonized_summary: Choose between squared error, Huber, or absolute error based on how many outliers the data has.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The error function that best handles the data's tail behavior.

provenance_notes: Excess kurtosis > 1.0 threshold: when kurtosis deviates significantly from the Gaussian baseline of 3 (excess > 1), squared-error estimates become exponentially sensitive to distributional tails.

Residual kurtosis is more informative than target kurtosis alone because it isolates the noise distribution from the signal; heavy-tailed targets with a good linear fit may still have light-tailed residuals.

Huber loss creates a piecewise function: quadratic for |error| < delta (MSE-like precision) and linear for |error| >= delta (MAE-like robustness). The delta parameter should be set dynamically from the 90th-95th percentile of baseline absolute residuals, not as a fixed scalar.
MAE is mathematically median-seeking rather than mean-seeking, making it inherently robust to extreme values without a tunable delta.
uncertainty_notes: If residuals are bimodal rather than simply heavy-tailed, both MAE and Huber may fail to capture the true central tendency; neither loss function models multimodal noise.

Huber delta is not scale-invariant: if y is not standardized before modeling, a static delta will trigger the quadratic-to-linear transition at an arbitrary point. Must compute delta dynamically via a robust scale estimator like MAD(residuals).

For asymmetric cost scenarios (e.g., under-prediction is costlier than over-prediction in insurance or finance), neither Huber nor MAE is appropriate; quantile/pinball loss is required to target a specific risk percentile.

records.summary: Recommend a linear model class and solver based on data characteristics.
records.dejargonized_summary: Pick the right linear model family and optimizer based on data size, sparsity, and target distribution.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The linear model family and solver that matches the data's distribution and scale.

provenance_notes: Dispersion index DI = Var(y)/E(y): DI = 1 strictly implies Poisson; DI > 1.1 indicates overdispersion requiring Tweedie or Negative Binomial.
Tweedie power parameter p: p=1 is Poisson, p=2 is Gamma, 1<p<2 is compound Poisson-Gamma (discrete point mass at zero plus continuous right-skewed tail, e.g. insurance claims).
newton-cholesky solver computes the explicit Hessian with O(p^2) space complexity; the p > 1000 threshold prevents catastrophic memory exhaustion.
sag (stochastic average gradient) avoids computing the full gradient at each step; saga extends sag to support non-smooth L1 penalties on sparse matrices.
Feature scaling must happen BEFORE solver execution: lbfgs and sag are notoriously sensitive to unscaled features where cross-feature variance differs by orders of magnitude.
uncertainty_notes: Underdispersion (DI < 1, variance less than mean) breaks both Poisson and Negative Binomial models; requires specialized distributions like Conway-Maxwell-Poisson which lack native sklearn implementations.
Tweedie power estimation via binned mean-variance regression is approximate and can be noisy for small datasets or targets with limited range.
If features are not standardized, sag and lbfgs gradients can explode numerically and the solver will fail to converge to the global minimum.

records.summary: Recommend a tree ensemble type based on sample size, categoricals, and noise.
records.dejargonized_summary: Choose between histogram boosting, random forest, or gradient boosting based on data size and noise level.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The tree ensemble architecture that best fits the data size and noise profile.

provenance_notes: n > 10,000 threshold: at this boundary sklearn HistGradientBoosting auto-enables early stopping; histogram binning reduces split-finding from O(n*p*log(n)) to O(n*bins), critical for large-scale deployment.

Bagging (RandomForest) trains independent deep trees on bootstrapped subsamples and averages predictions; this targets variance reduction without increasing bias, making it resilient to noisy or corrupted data.
Boosting (GradientBoosting) trains weak shallow learners sequentially on the negative gradient of the accumulated ensemble; this targets bias reduction but is susceptible to memorizing noise.
HistGradientBoosting discretizes continuous features into up to 256 integer bins, making split-finding CPU cache-friendly and fundamentally faster on high-dimensional data.
uncertainty_notes: HistGradientBoosting natively handles categoricals as non-ordered nominal quantities, but encounters severe performance degradation or memory spikes when categorical cardinality is extreme (thousands of unique values); target encoding must precede the ensemble in those cases.

All tree-based ensembles are mathematically incapable of extrapolation: if the target exhibits trends beyond the training range (e.g., upward time series), trees will flatline predictions at the maximum observed training value. Linear models are required for extrapolation tasks.

The noise-level threshold between bagging and boosting is soft and estimated from a shallow tree proxy; the boundary is not sharp and domain context should inform the choice at intermediate noise levels.

records.summary: Recommend preprocessing transformations based on feature diagnostics.
records.dejargonized_summary: Decide which scaling, transforms, and feature removal steps the data needs before modeling.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The data preparation steps that fix distributional and collinearity problems.

provenance_notes: |skewness| > 1.0 threshold: features outside [-1, 1] have high asymmetry that violates normality assumptions in gradient descent and isotropic distance metrics (KNN, SVC, K-Means).
VIF_j = 1/(1-R_j^2): VIF > 5 means moderate collinearity, VIF > 10 means the variance of coefficient j is inflated tenfold purely by linear dependence on other variables.
Box-Cox transform uses logarithms and is mathematically undefined for x <= 0; a deterministic system must detect non-positive values and override to Yeo-Johnson.

StandardScaler(with_mean=True) on a sparse document-term matrix replaces structural zeros with dense negative values, instantly destroying sparsity and causing catastrophic RAM exhaustion. Must use MaxAbsScaler or with_mean=False.
RFE (Recursive Feature Elimination) has computational complexity O(n * p * step) because it re-evaluates the model at each elimination step.
uncertainty_notes: Skewness threshold is conventional, not derived from a sharp statistical boundary; tree-based models tolerate skew well while distance-based models do not.
VIF is undefined or misleading when p >= n; cannot be computed for wide datasets and should be skipped in favor of direct regularization.
When all features exceed VIF > 10, the collinearity is total and VIF-based removal offers no selective guidance; dimensionality reduction (PCA) is the only viable path.

records.summary: Recommend dimensionality reduction based on condition number and sparsity.
records.dejargonized_summary: Decide whether to reduce dimensions with PCA or TruncatedSVD, or skip it entirely.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: Whether the feature space needs compressing and which method preserves the right structure.

provenance_notes: PCA performs eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix, producing strictly orthogonal components that eliminate multicollinearity entirely: condition number of the transformed subspace is exactly 1.

0.90/0.95/0.99 explained variance cutoffs are industry-standard; passing n_components=0.95 to sklearn PCA dynamically selects the minimal eigenvector count to preserve exactly 95% of spectral variance.
TruncatedSVD operates directly on the uncentered matrix, preserving sparsity that PCA's required mean-centering step would destroy.

condition_number is shared with regularization_selection: high condition number may be resolved by either regularization or dimensionality reduction, and the architect must choose the appropriate intervention.
uncertainty_notes: PCA is a linear transformation that only captures global linear variance. If data lies on a nonlinear manifold (e.g., Swiss Roll), PCA will collapse classes on top of each other, destroying local neighborhoods.

Manifold learning alternatives (t-SNE, UMAP, Isomap) are strictly transductive: they map existing points but lack a parametric transform for out-of-sample data, making them inappropriate as preprocessors for predictive pipelines.
Explained variance threshold is conventional, not derived from a principled criterion; in some domains 0.90 retention may discard critical discriminative variance.

records.summary: Recommend hyperparameter search ranges for a given model type.
records.dejargonized_summary: Set smart starting ranges for tuning knobs based on the model type and data size.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The initial search boundaries for model tuning that avoid wasted compute.

provenance_notes: sklearn Lasso/ElasticNet cost function scales the residual sum of squares by 1/(2n), making the optimal alpha mathematically invariant to sample size. This allows standardized log-space grids without per-dataset recalibration.

Gradient boosting prediction is updated sequentially as f += learning_rate * tree_prediction; there is a strict inverse tradeoff between learning_rate and n_estimators: halving lr requires doubling n_estimators for equivalent capacity.
learning_rate < 0.125 yields diminishing returns in accuracy while linearly increasing n_estimators and compute time (Friedman 1999).

Misclassification error on standard tabular datasets frequently flatlines after ~200 estimators when lr is sufficiently tuned; searching beyond this asymptote yields statistically unstable and slightly overfitting configurations.
model_type is determined by upstream regularization_selection or tree_ensemble_selection decisions; the architect must ensure those atoms run before this one.
uncertainty_notes: alpha=0 entirely bypasses regularized solvers, forcing the algorithm back to unregularized OLS; sklearn documentation advises against this due to floating-point instability. The hard floor at 1e-5 prevents this collapse.
Grid ranges are heuristic starting points: if the optimal parameter sits at a grid boundary, the grid itself is likely miscalibrated and should be expanded.
The lr/n_estimators tradeoff assumes standard tabular data; for highly structured domains (images, graphs) the asymptotic behavior may differ.

records.dejargonized_summary: Pick the right way to split the data for testing so that error estimates are honest.

heuristic.dejargonized_meaning: The data splitting method that prevents leakage and gives reliable error estimates.

provenance_notes: Standard KFold assigns samples to folds arbitrarily, assuming i.i.d. data with zero memory of past states. Temporal data violates this: future data points leak into training folds, allowing prediction of past events using future knowledge.

StratifiedKFold ensures exact class proportions are maintained across folds; without this, a rare class (e.g., 1% anomaly) might be entirely absent from a validation fold, making precision and ROC-AUC mathematically undefined.

LOOCV uses n-1 training samples per fold, maximizing data utilization. But because the n training sets overlap by n-2 samples, the trained models are highly correlated, generating high variance in the performance estimate despite near-zero bias.

Single-loop CV for a hyperparameter-tuned model yields up to 30% optimistic error inflation on null datasets (Varma & Simon 2006); nested CV isolates tuning in an inner loop and estimation in an outer loop to eliminate this bias.
is_timeseries is determined by check_time_series_index from the diagnostics family; has_groups requires domain metadata not derivable from the design matrix alone.
uncertainty_notes: If multiple records originate from the same entity (e.g., multiple scans from one patient, multiple transactions from one user), standard CV randomization will place same-entity records in both train and test, creating massive leakage. GroupKFold must be used but requires group labels as external metadata.

LOOCV is mathematically invalid for time series because leaving a single isolated time-step out destroys contiguous temporal relationships required for autoregressive processing; walk-forward validation must be used instead.

n <= 100 LOOCV threshold is a computational viability boundary (requires fitting n models), not a statistical optimality boundary; RepeatedKFold may be preferable for variance reduction even at small n.
